title: The other World Cup
gist: Australia's $600 million, ten-year PNG Chiefs rugby league project is a soft-power bet whose real test, the author argues, is the under-funded women's game — with only $6 million a year going to Team Up sport-for-development programs versus $250 million for elite community/development programs — and he proposes ring-fencing 5% of major sport-diplomacy investments for women's community competition and safeguarding.

insights.claim: The PNG Chiefs NRL franchise, underwritten by $600 million in Australian government funding over ten years, has spent 2026 signing marquee names ahead of its 2028 NRL debut, but the author argues Canberra's investment will ultimately be judged not by premierships but by whether Pacific women can play, earn and lead in the sport.
insights.speaker: Darren Coughlan
insights.so_what: Frames the $600m Chiefs investment as a soft-power project whose success metric investors/policymakers should track is gender-inclusive participation and leadership, not just on-field results.
insights.quote: Canberra's investment will not ultimately be judged by whether a franchise wins premierships. It will be judged by whether Pacific women can now play, earn and lead in the game Papua New Guinea calls its own.
insights.locator: But the sharper test of Australia's Pacific sport statecraft

insights.claim: Australia's sport-diplomacy model in the Pacific (patient, people-focused investment in participation) is presented as a deliberate contrast to China's 'stadium diplomacy,' exemplified by the 10,000-seat arena China built in Honiara, Solomon Islands for the 2023 Pacific Games.
insights.speaker: Darren Coughlan
insights.so_what: Illustrates a China-Australia soft-power competition dynamic in the Pacific playing out through sport infrastructure versus grassroots participation programs — a useful frame for tracking Pacific-islands influence competition.
insights.quote: China's stadium diplomacy handed Honiara a 10,000-seat arena for the 2023 Pacific Games. Australia is betting instead on the people who fill grounds like it.

themes.theme: Women's rugby league infrastructure being built

insights.claim: The Santos Cup, PNG's first national women's rugby league competition, is mid-season with six provincial franchises, an extended preseason, tiered player contracts and fixtures from Port Moresby to Rabaul, backed by PacificAus Sports; five of its head and assistant coaches this season are women.
insights.speaker: Darren Coughlan
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of real institution-building in PNG women's sport, not just rhetoric — a leading indicator of whether the broader Chiefs project's gender-equity goals are being met on the ground.
insights.locator: The encouraging news is that something real is being built

insights.claim: Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade Team Up program, comprising over 35 sport-for-development partnerships, engaged more than 112,000 Pacific Islanders in its most recent reported year, with women and girls holding steady at 42% to 47% of participants.
insights.speaker: Darren Coughlan
entities: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale and gender balance of Australia's flagship Pacific sport-development program, a baseline metric for evaluating future funding increases.
insights.locator: Across the region, the title-winning Fijiana Drua

themes.theme: What the research evidence says about sport-for-development

insights.claim: An umbrella review of violence prevention interventions found sport-based programs produced the strongest effects of any approach, but reviews of sport-for-development consistently find gains concentrated at the individual level (confidence, skills, income) with no documented case of a sport program shifting gender equality at the structural level.
insights.speaker: Darren Coughlan
insights.so_what: Sets realistic expectations for sport-diplomacy ROI: individual empowerment outcomes are well evidenced, but investors/policymakers should not expect sport programs alone to shift structural gender inequality.
insights.quote: no documented case of a sport program shifting gender equality at the structural level
insights.locator: The research record says this work is worth doing

insights.claim: The most rigorous trial in the field, a football-based program in Peru, cut partner violence against adolescent girls by 75% even as inequitable gender attitudes rose among participants — evidence that behavioural progress from sport programs can be real but non-linear and does not necessarily track attitude change.
insights.speaker: Darren Coughlan
insights.so_what: A specific, high-confidence data point (75% reduction) that should temper simplistic narratives about sport programs 'changing culture' — outcomes can be strong on behavior while attitudes lag.
insights.quote: cut partner violence against adolescent girls by 75% even as inequitable gender attitudes rose
insights.locator: Even the field's most rigorous trial

insights.claim: Sport is not automatically a safe environment for women: studies report that 26% to 74% of women in sport experience gender-based interpersonal violence, meaning participation pathways without safeguarding can harm the very people they are meant to serve.
insights.speaker: Darren Coughlan
insights.so_what: A material risk factor for any sport-diplomacy program expansion — safeguarding investment is not optional overhead but a core requirement, given the high reported prevalence range of abuse in sport settings.
insights.quote: 26% to 74% of women in sport experience gender-based interpersonal violence
insights.locator: And sport is not automatically a safe place

insights.claim: The most recent Pacific-specific evidence, from Fiji, shows sport operating as a gendered livelihood pathway, with women's participation constrained by domestic responsibilities and community norms.
insights.speaker: Darren Coughlan
insights.so_what: Region-specific evidence that structural barriers (domestic labor burden, social norms), not just funding or facilities, limit women's participation in Pacific sport — relevant for designing effective program interventions.
insights.locator: The most recent Pacific evidence, from Fiji

themes.theme: Funding imbalance and the policy proposal

insights.claim: Within the $600 million PNG Chiefs package, $250 million is earmarked for development and community programs across PNG, Fiji, Samoa and Tonga, yet Team Up — the flagship program doing the daily work of participation and inclusion across the whole region — runs on roughly $6 million a year, a stark funding imbalance relative to elite franchise spending.
insights.speaker: Darren Coughlan
insights.so_what: Quantifies a roughly 40:1 imbalance between elite-franchise-adjacent development spending and grassroots inclusion programming — a concrete budget-allocation gap for Australian sport-diplomacy policymakers to address.
insights.locator: That is where the imbalance bites

insights.claim: A 2025 audit by the Gendered Violence Research Network at the University of New South Wales, mapping 31 violence-prevention programs delivered through Australian sport, found persistent gaps for First Nations, culturally diverse and remote communities, and reliance on untrained volunteers to carry safeguarding responsibilities.
insights.speaker: Darren Coughlan
insights.so_what: Documents an existing systemic weakness (volunteer-reliant, undertrained safeguarding) in Australia's domestic sport-violence-prevention programs that is likely to recur if Pacific programs are scaled without dedicated safeguarding funding.
insights.locator: A 2025 audit by the Gendered Violence Research Network

insights.claim: The author proposes that before the October 2026 World Cup, Canberra should ring-fence 5% of every major elite sport-diplomacy investment for women's community competition and independent safeguarding, co-designed and delivered through Pacific bodies rather than administered from Australia — on the PNG package alone this would be $30 million, five times Team Up's annual budget and a rounding error against franchise spend.
insights.speaker: Darren Coughlan
insights.so_what: A specific, costed policy proposal ($30 million, 5% ring-fence) that gives a concrete number to track for whether Australia follows through on gender-equitable Pacific sport diplomacy ahead of the October 2026 World Cup deadline.
insights.quote: ring-fence 5% of every major elite sport diplomacy investment for women's community competition and independent safeguarding
